title: My Father Married A Woman He Met At A Grief Support Group Eight Months After My Mother Died, And Two Weeks After His Funeral The Insurance Company Told Me His $400,000 Policy Was Changed To Her While He Lay On Morphine In Hospice, Witnessed

blocks.text: PART 1 — FORTY-SIX YEARS

My parents, Tom and Linda Gallagher, were married for forty-six years. They met at a church dance in Scranton, Pennsylvania, in 1972. Dad was a lineman for the electric company. Mom was a school secretary. They raised two kids, me and my younger brother Patrick, in a small white house with a basketball hoop over the garage.

Dad was the kind of father who showed his love through planning. He changed the oil in our cars until we were thirty. He kept a binder labeled “IMPORTANT” in his desk drawer with every insurance policy, deed, and account number the family had. And he bought a life insurance policy in 1993, the year Patrick was born. Four hundred thousand dollars.
“If anything happens to me,” he told us at least a hundred times, “you two and your mother are taken care of. It’s all in the binder.”

When Mom died of a stroke in 2021, the beneficiaries on Dad’s policy were already Patrick and me. He’d changed it years earlier so that, after Mom, everything would come straight to us. He showed us the paperwork himself. He made us both read it.

After Mom died, Dad was lost. He didn’t know how to cook. He didn’t know how to be alone in that quiet house. My brother and I called him every day, but we both lived hours away. I’m in Philadelphia, and Patrick’s in Pittsburgh.
So when Dad joined a grief support group at a church in town, we were relieved. And when he told us, eight months later, that he’d met someone there, we tried to be happy for him.

Her name was Sheila. She was sixty-two, a widow, warm and talkative. She called Dad “Tommy” and made him laugh again. They were married at the courthouse in the spring of 2022, just eight months after they met.
I’m Erin. I’m fifty. I’m a dental hygienist. I want to be fair to Sheila: at first, I liked her.
If anything happens to me, you two and your mother are taken care of. It’s all in the binder.
PART 2 — THE DIAGNOSIS
In the summer of 2023, Dad was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. It was already advanced.

He went through a round of treatment that made him terribly sick and didn’t help much. By September, his doctors recommended hospice. He moved into an inpatient hospice facility in October, when his pain became too hard to manage at home.
Patrick and I took turns driving in every weekend. During the week, Sheila was with him. She was there every day. I’ll admit I felt guilty about that, and grateful.

By October, Dad was on morphine around the clock. He slept almost all the time, maybe twenty hours a day. When he was awake, he was foggy and confused. He called the nurses by Mom’s name. He asked me once if Patrick had finished his homework. Patrick was thirty.

One Saturday, he looked at my daughter, his granddaughter, and asked her name. He had known her for nineteen years. She held his hand and told him, and he smiled and said, “That’s a pretty name.” Then he fell back asleep.
He died on a Thursday in March, peacefully, with Sheila, Patrick, and me in the room.

The funeral was at the church where he and Mom were married. The lineman crew from his old company came in their work trucks and parked them in a line outside the church. Patrick gave the eulogy. I couldn’t.
Two weeks later, I called the insurance company to start the claim. I had the policy number from Dad’s binder. I had the death certificate. I figured it would be a simple phone call.
The woman on the phone was very polite. She asked for my name. She typed for a moment. Then she paused for a long time.
“Ma’am,” she said, “you’re not the beneficiary on this policy.”
Ma’am, you’re not the beneficiary on this policy.
PART 3 — OCTOBER
I thought she’d made a mistake. I gave her the policy number again. I told her I had a copy of the beneficiary designation in my father’s own files, naming me and my brother.
“I see that designation in our records,” she said. “But it was changed last year. We received a change of beneficiary form in October.”
She hesitated, then said, “The current primary beneficiary is Sheila Gallagher. One hundred percent.”
I asked her to tell me the date. She did. I asked her to repeat it. I wrote it on the back of an envelope. I looked at it three times.
October. Dad had moved into hospice the first week of October. The form was dated October seventeenth.
On October seventeenth, my father was in a hospice bed on a morphine pump. He was sleeping twenty hours a day. He didn’t know his own granddaughter’s name.

I asked the woman how the form had been sent in. She looked it up. It had been faxed from a fax number at the hospice facility, she said. It had Dad’s signature. And it had a witness signature, from someone who identified herself as a hospice nurse.
She read it to me. A name I’d never heard. Something like “Karen D. Wilson, RN.”

I spent nearly every weekend at that hospice for five months. I knew every nurse on Dad’s unit. I knew their names, their kids’ names, which ones brought in cookies. There was no nurse named Karen Wilson.
I thanked the insurance company representative, hung up, and called the hospice.
On October seventeenth, my father was in a hospice bed on a morphine pump.
PART 4 — THEY NEVER HEARD OF HER
The hospice’s director of nursing was a gentle woman named Marianne. She had sat with our family the night Dad died. She remembered me immediately.
I told her what the insurance company had said. I asked if they had a nurse named Karen Wilson.

She checked. She came back on the phone a few minutes later. “Erin, we’ve never had anyone by that name on our staff,” she said. “Not on Tom’s unit. Not anywhere in this facility. Not now, not in the past.”

I asked her about the fax. She said patients and families sometimes use the fax machine at the nurses’ station to send insurance and medical forms. A staff member usually helps them. She couldn’t tell me who had sent that particular fax without checking.
“Marianne,” I said, “would my father have been able to sign anything on October seventeenth?”
She was quiet. Then she said she couldn’t discuss his medical condition without proper authorization, but that I could request his records as his next of kin. Then she said something else, carefully.

“I’ll tell you this, Erin. If a patient on our unit was going to sign a legal document, our policy is that our social worker is informed, and that a staff member assesses whether the patient is alert enough to understand it. I have no record of anything like that for your father.”
I hung up and called Patrick in Pittsburgh. He didn’t say anything for a long time. Then he said the thing neither of us wanted to say out loud.
“Sheila,” he said. “Sheila was there every day.”
“I don’t either,” I said. “But somebody faxed that form from Dad’s hospice.”
Erin, we’ve never had anyone by that name on our staff.
PART 5 — THE RECORDS
I’m not a lawyer. But I’m a dental hygienist, and I know how medical charts work. So the first thing I did was request Dad’s hospice records, as his next of kin and the executor of his will.
They came three weeks later. Hundreds of pages. I read every one of them on my kitchen table, with a cup of coffee and a highlighter.
October seventeenth was there in black and white.
“Patient sleeping most of shift. Arousable to voice but drifts back to sleep. Oriented to self only. Not oriented to place or time.”
Oriented to self only. That’s a medical way of saying Dad knew his own name, but not where he was or what day it was.
The morphine doses were listed. The nurses’ names were listed. Every nurse who cared for him that day signed their notes. None of them was named Karen Wilson.

There was also a note from the social worker, dated a few days earlier. She had met with “patient’s wife” to discuss “advance directives and paperwork.” Sheila had told the social worker that “all financial matters are in order.” The social worker had written: “Wife declined assistance with any legal documents.”

Next, I asked the insurance company for a copy of the change form. They said they could only give it to the beneficiary or to the estate’s legal representative. As executor, I was the estate’s representative. After some back and forth, they sent it.
The form had Dad’s name typed in. The new beneficiary, Sheila, typed in. Then two signatures at the bottom.
The first was supposed to be Dad’s. It was shaky and slanted, nothing like the strong, neat signature from his binder. The second was the “witness” signature. “Karen D. Wilson, RN.”
I held the form next to a birthday card Sheila had sent me the previous year. I looked at the capital W. And the way the “n” trailed off at the end.
